sixLiteralCanonicalGroups.individualGround: PRlib L46–55 explicitly links the Soviet government’s 1918 relocation from Petrograd to Moscow; L52 names that origin, so key0 follows the source independently of the frozen index. All four labels are cities, consistently standalone nominative labels, with no answer-length or grammatical key cue. Novgorod and Kyiv invite confusion with old political centers; Nizhny Novgorod is a comparable Russian city/name-confusion option. None can also satisfy the particular 1918 transfer explicitly named by the source.

sixLiteralCanonicalGroups.literal: Советское правительство перенесло столицу из Петрограда в Москву: 12 марта 1918 года Москва вновь стала столицей Советского государства. 16 марта IV Всероссийский съезд Советов временно закрепил этот перенос.
sixLiteralCanonicalGroups.individualGround: The first sentence names Petrograd and Moscow and states 12 March 1918, matching PRlib L52–54. The second sentence gives 16 March, IV All-Russian Congress and a temporary decision, matching the complete resolution context L55. It neither says the transfer was originally permanent nor conflates the unfulfilled 1917 plan with the actual 1918 move.

sixLiteralCanonicalGroups.literal: Правительственные учреждения должны были переехать из Петрограда в Москву 11–12 марта 1918 года.
sixLiteralCanonicalGroups.individualGround: PRlib L52 explicitly states that all government institutions were to move from Petrograd to Moscow on 11–12 March. The note preserves the normative wording “должны были” rather than claiming every institution physically completed relocation then. Exact planned days add a concrete fact about the keyed city’s evacuation beyond origin city/year in the prompt.

sixLiteralCanonicalGroups.literal: Великий Новгород — древний русский город на реке Волхов.
sixLiteralCanonicalGroups.individualGround: The Novgorod state museum identifies Veliky Novgorod, describes the ancient city and medieval Rus monuments in L217–220, and explicitly crosses the Volkhov to the city’s other side. This supports the independent city/river fact; it does not attribute the 1918 capital move to Novgorod.

sixLiteralCanonicalGroups.literal: Нижний Новгород — административный центр Нижегородской области. Он расположен при слиянии Волги и Оки.
sixLiteralCanonicalGroups.individualGround: The MCHS regional description L205–206 explicitly names Nizhny Novgorod as the oblast’s administrative center and places it at the Volga/Oka confluence. Both independent clauses in the note are supported, useful for identifying this city, and do not confuse it with Veliky Novgorod.

absoluteLevel.ground: Requires identifying the Soviet government’s former seat under the historical name Petrograd in the specific 1918 move, rather than naming today’s capital or merely recalling the city founded by Peter. A reader familiar with revolutionary Russian history recognizes it; a non-specialist can confuse old Russian political centers/epochs or the two Novgorods. This is lower-edge thematic historical familiarity, not an obscure expert date; the date is supplied rather than tested. No linguistic or answer-format cue singles out key0. Difficulty is editorial, not a measured human outcome.
